Hospital command center: census, early warning and margin in a simulated health system

How full will the hospital get, who is about to deteriorate, and what does it cost?

Simulated health system: Calloway Bay Health is fictional, a 500-bed medical center plus five offsite sites (710 inpatient beds in all). Census, weather, patients and finances are synthetic, with planted parameters so each step can be checked. 500 Monte Carlo paths per scenario; seed 20261123. Drive it yourself in the Command Center prototype.

Headline: Calloway Bay's main campus runs at 78% occupancy in a normal week, but its medicine floors run at 94%. A respiratory surge is the hardest week: the median peak reaches 88% and the main ED spends 58 h on diversion. Continuous monitoring with a sustained NEWS2 alert catches 85% of planted deteriorations vs 64% for 4-hourly checks, and the system earns a 3.1% operating margin over a simulated year.

  • 78%Main-campus inpatient occupancy, normal week
  • 23%Chance the peak tops 90% in a respiratory surge
  • 1.8 hMedian warning before a deterioration (continuous, sustained NEWS2 ≥ 5)
  • 3.1%Operating margin over a simulated year

Findings

  • The medicine floors are the bottleneck. In a baseline week the three medicine units average 94% full and sit at 95% or more 55% of the time, while the main campus overall averages 78%. Even so, ED boarding stays modest (median weekly peak 3 patients) because overflow to sister units absorbs most surges.
  • A respiratory surge does the most damage. With the respiratory index climbing to its January level, occupancy averages 82%, the median peak hits 88% (90th percentile 91%), ED boarders peak at 10, the ED is on diversion 58 h of the week (vs 12 h) and 23 transfers are declined. Extra volume still raises the week's operating income by $960.0K, net of $129.1K more agency spend.
  • Short shocks are absorbed. The heat wave lifts the peak to 85% and diversion to 23 h; the mass-casualty incident pushes the main-campus ICUs to a median peak of 94% (vs 89%). The blizzard costs money despite similar census: cancelled surgery and staff call-outs move operating income by −$370.4K.
  • Continuous monitoring buys warning, at an alarm cost. Spot checks every 4 hours with the standard NEWS2 trigger alert on 64% of planted deteriorations, a median 2.3 h ahead. Continuous readings with the same trigger catch 99% but raise 156 false-alert episodes per 100 patient-days; requiring NEWS2 ≥ 5 for an hour keeps 85% (+21 pts over spot checks) at 2.4 false alerts and a 1.8 h median lead. qSOFA flags 46% of sepsis cases on spot checks and 99% continuously.
  • Forecasts are honest. Backtested over 118 daily origins in a simulated truth path, the 80% band contained the actual census 81% of the time a day ahead and 76% three days ahead; the median missed by 11.9 patients at 72 h vs 18.5 for assuming tomorrow looks like today.
  • The morning huddle can see tomorrow's discharges. A logistic model on huddle-time features (days in vs expected stay, discharge order, vital signs, oxygen, weekend) ranks who leaves in 24 hours with AUC 0.90, against 0.85 for the discharge-order flag alone, and is calibrated (slope 0.98). Summed by unit, it misses daily discharges by 0.8 patients vs 1.7 for a census-over-length-of-stay estimate.
  • The year earns 3.1%, and the busy months earn the most. Net patient revenue is $1,100.1M on $3,054.2M of charges. The best month is February (6.9%) and the worst May (1.3%): winter volume spreads fixed costs further than the overtime and agency premium it requires. Overtime and agency are 13.3% of nursing spend over the year.

Discharge prediction

29,857 simulated stays across every inpatient unit, snapshotted at 07:00 each day (75,654 training and 32,479 test snapshots, split by patient); 27% of snapshots end in a discharge within 24 hours. Stays are planted: length of stay depends on the unit, diagnosis group weight, age and elective status; discharges happen 10:00–18:00 and some weekend discharges slip to Monday; 75% get a discharge order 2–30 hours ahead, and 15% of those slip a day anyway.

Method

Each hour, every unit u with nu patients not already waiting for a bed discharges or transfers Eu~Binomial(nu,hu) of them, with a hazard set by its mean stay Lu, the hour-of-week discharge weight wu (mean 1; discharges cluster late morning and slow at weekends) and the environment's length-of-stay multiplier ℓu:

hu(t)=1−exp(−wu(t)Luℓu(t)),(Eu→v)v~Multinomial(Eu,πu)

Patients routed to a full unit keep their current bed (boarding) until a bed or an overflow unit opens; higher-acuity and perioperative patients are placed first. New arrivals are Au~Poisson(λu(t)mu(t)): an ED never refuses walk-ins but diverts its ambulance share once patients reach 1.10× its bays, the ORs queue cases for a free room, and other units decline transfers when they and their overflow units are full.

The environment multiplies arrivals by a seasonal respiratory index R(t), heat above 92°F and snow:

mu(t)=(1+kρu(R(t)−1))(1+ηθumax(0,T(t)−T*))(1−σus0(t))(1+αus1(t))

with unit sensitivities ρ,θ,σ,α, snow severity today s0 and over the previous two days s1 (inches/12, capped at 1), k=0.35 and η=0.012. NEWS2 (RCP 2017, SpO2 scale 1) and qSOFA (Seymour et al., 2016) are computed from simulated readings with measurement noise; nursing cost follows each unit's patients-per-RN ratio, with core staff budgeted to a target occupancy and anything above it paid at 1.5× (overtime, up to 12% of core hours) or 2.4× (agency).

Assumptions

  • Charges, payer mixes, collection rates (Medicare 30%, Medicaid 24%, commercial 56%, self-pay 7% of charges), costs and nurse ratios are invented but sized for a US system of this scale. Fixed costs per bed were set so the baseline year lands near a typical 2–4% margin; the margin's level is an assumption, its swings across scenarios and months are model output.
  • Core RN cost $62/h loaded. Weather and the respiratory season are synthetic curves, not NOAA or CDC data.
  • The command-center model is unit-level: it tracks counts of patients, not diagnoses or individual paths, so it can't speak to clinical outcomes.

Caveats

  • Lengths of stay are memoryless within each unit (exponential hazards shaped by time of day), which understates how predictable long stays are; real forecasting would use expected discharge dates.
  • Early-warning results depend on the planted deterioration shapes and noise levels; they show the trade-off's direction, not real-world sensitivities.
  • Diversion, staffing and boarding rules are simplified; real command centers juggle many more levers (surge beds, discharge lounges, transfer agreements).
